verdict.reasoning: Patient: "it seems to have been slowly getting worse over the last couple of weeks. It's become quite troublesome the last few days."

Patient: "Normally I can walk to the shops without a problem, but now I'm having to sort of sit down and catch my breath and I'm even starting to get a bit breathless just about the house" – indicates breathless with minimal exertion and at home.
Patient: "I've got a bit of a dry cough, but it's not too troublesome." – a mild dry cough.

Patient: "I've noticed my ankles have gotten bigger... It's just like they've sort of swollen up a bit." and "Yeah, both ankles" and "I kind of noticed it the last few days." – bilateral ankle swelling for a few days.
Patient: "I think my ankles did swell up a bit last time. The heart failure was a problem." – prior ankle swelling with past heart failure problems.
Patient denies chest pain: "No pain in my chest." Denies palpitations: "No, not really." Denies fever: "No."
Patient: "I'm feeling a little run down, but otherwise otherwise pretty normal." – mild fatigue and otherwise feels well.
Doctor: "And how about your appetite? Are you eating and drinking? Okay." Patient: "Yeah, that's fine." – normal appetite.
Doctor: "And your water works? Are you passing urine? Okay." Patient: "Yeah." – indicates urination is okay/normal.
Patient adds: "Yeah, I usually pee a lot." – reports frequent urination.
Patient: "I've. I've got heart failure." and later doctor summarizes heart failure history.
Patient: "I was told I had, like. They called it, like, a small heart attack about five years ago." – consistent with small myocardial infarction ~5 years ago.

Transcript mentions a "small heart attack" but never explicitly states ischemic heart disease or links it as a formal diagnosis; inferring a coded history of ischemic heart disease is an added interpretation.

Doctor: "apart from your diuretics that you're taking?" Patient: "Yeah, I take something called furosemide." Doctor: "And do you know which dose you're taking?" Patient: "I can't remember." – taking furosemide, dose unknown.
Patient: "Yeah, I take aspirin." – dose not discussed, so dose unknown.
Doctor: "Metoprolol. Was this. Sorry, the connection is not very good. Okay, thank you." – indicates metoprolol is among medications; dose not stated.
Patient: "Simvastatin." after metoprolol is clarified – taking simvastatin; no dose given.
Doctor: "Any allergies at all? Any medications?" Patient: "No, no allergies." – no known drug allergies.
Patient: "My father died of a heart attack." Doctor: "How old was your father when he passed away?" Patient: "He was early 60s."
Patient: "My mother had osteoporosis." Doctor: "Is your mother still with us?" Patient: "Yeah, she's still living."
Patient: "I live on my own. I got two cats." and "They're called Polly and Tim."
Patient: "I work part time as a lorry driver." and later confirms only day shifts: "Oh, no, I only take shifts during the day."

Doctor: "Do you smoke at all?" Patient: "Not anymore." "So you used to smoke?" "Yeah." "How many did you smoke a day on average?" "Oh, it was about a pack a day back in the day." "And how many years was that for?" "Oh, that was a good 25 years." – ~25 pack-years.
Doctor: "And what about alcohol?" Patient: "I don't drink alcohol."
Doctor: "Do you do much in the way of exercise, sir?" Patient: "I try and walk to the shops least once a day. But that's about it." – minimal exercise.

Doctor: "given that you're otherwise well at the moment and having examined you, your chest and your saturations and blood pressure, all. Okay" – details not provided but chest, sats, and BP reported as okay/normal.
Doctor: "I wonder whether you've had a flare up of your heart failure, sir, which can sometimes happen." – heart failure exacerbation as primary assessment.

Doctor recap: "you've been feeling breathless... you mentioned you had a bit of a dry cough and some swelling in your ankles" and later attributes symptoms to heart failure "flare up" – consistent with HF exacerbation presenting with SOB, edema, and cough (fluid overload).

As with pmh-003, the transcript mentions a "small heart attack" but does not explicitly record a diagnosis of ischemic heart disease; labeling it as a history of ischemic heart disease is an extrapolated diagnosis.
Medication adherence is not discussed, so it is unclear. For dose: Doctor: "And do you know which dose you're taking?" Patient: "I can't remember." – furosemide dose needs clarification.

Doctor: "quite happy to increase your dose of Frozamide. So maybe rather than one tablet day, we can give you two tablets a day" and later "increase your frusamide to one tablet twice a day." No specific strength (e.g., 40 mg) is mentioned, so stating "40 mg twice daily" adds an unsupported specific dose.

Doctor: "let's get a blood test done. We can check your full blood count, look for signs of anemia, we can have a check your kidney function" – CBC and renal function to look for anemia and kidney status; electrolytes are typically part of kidney function labs and not contradicted.
Doctor: "what we should also think about is maybe doing a couple of other tests, like a blood test and Maybe an echocardiogram of your heart... That's something I can organize for you today."
Doctor: "I really would like you to come back and see me in about a week's time to see how you're getting on." – follow-up in 1 week to reassess symptoms/response.

Doctor: "if you are getting more unwell, so if you're getting more breathless or you're having any other symptoms like chest pain or palpitations or dizziness, then, you know, I want you to give me a call sooner" – advice to report sooner with worsening symptoms.
Same as plan-004: "come back and see me in about a week's time to see how you're getting on."
Same as plan-005: instruction to contact sooner for worsening shortness of breath, chest pain, palpitations, or dizziness.

Opening: Patient: "I'm contacting you because I've been quite short of breath lately." and describes it "slowly getting worse over the last couple of weeks." – gradually worsening shortness of breath as chief complaint.
